notes: claimId 'dossier' means the sentence rests on dossier text with no matching ledger quote; fact-checker should verify against the listed URL. Uncited sentences that carry caveats (not peer-reviewed, not reproduced) come from dossier status labels and caller instructions.

citations.sentence: Anthropic on Nov. 2 released FlashProve, an open-source prototype that attaches a cryptographic proof to an AI model's reply.
Anthropic says the proof shows the reply came from a model the provider committed to in advance.
This is a company research post, not peer-reviewed. We found no independent reproduction of its numbers.
citations.note: Rewritten per factcheck fix; uncited negative softened to 'we found no'.

citations.sentence: Anthropic writes that a user today "cannot check that the responses came from the specific model ... for cost reasons".
First, the provider publishes a commitment, a short fingerprint of one exact set of weights, the numbers a model learns in training.
Anthropic says this step takes about 39 minutes and covers about 16 million requests.
Anyone with the commitment, prompt and reply can check it on a CPU in about 17 seconds using 24 threads (21 seconds on one thread).
claimIds: factcheck: '17 seconds on 24 threads', 21 s single-thread

citations.sentence: The proofs hide the weights but not the architecture, the model's overall design.
Anthropic tested a 400-billion-parameter open model, Llama 4 Maverick, not Claude.
It credits Claude with the speedups: "Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference".
Table: Proofs arrive at about 110 tokens per second on one H100 GPU, about 19 MB each.
Table: Proving costs about 70 to 95 times the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM serving software.
claimIds: factcheck: '~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM'

citations.sentence: Table: the only earlier proof of the same model Anthropic knows of took 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens. (Evidence column: 'That comparison also comes from Anthropic's post.')
Table: "A provider can commit to any model it likes, a small or degenerate one included".
Table: The weights stay hidden.
Table: "We expect, rather than know, that the programs hide the weights".
Table: Timing attacks are out of scope.
Table: Only the slow Lean verifier is proved correct. The fast C++ verifier used day to day "carries no formal guarantee".
An independent paper posted to arXiv in July and accepted to the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy makes a related point about such systems.
claimIds: factcheck: arXiv abs comments 'Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P 2026)'; date 2026-07-30

citations.sentence: It predates FlashProve and does not examine it.
claimIds: factcheck fix wording; paper dated 2026-07-30, FlashProve released 2026-11-02

citations.sentence: It argues a dishonest provider could keep "the declared architecture and parameter count" while embedding "ghost weights" that do far less work.
Its authors conclude that "proof of correct inference is not proof of large-model execution".
Proofs cover an integer version of the model, and Anthropic says real floating-point or sampled replies "could depart at some position".
In one repository test, the top predicted token differed at 6.81% of positions.
Contexts are capped at 1,024 tokens, which Anthropic calls "quite short" next to chat sessions.
Two published attacks on Fiat–Shamir, a method these proofs rely on, "have not been examined against this protocol".
TechCrunch reports "no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab".
the code is labeled "not maintained, not accepting contributions".
Anthropic calls the release "intermediate progress" and asks others to "take it, and improve it".
It plans to hide architecture details next.
All 18 AI models tested on a new 240-task teamwork benchmark show "clear weaknesses as a teammate," and the best scored only 82.2 out of 100.
This one grades a single model as a member of a team, across 8 dimensions "from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work that a weaker model leaves behind".
models are scored only on tasks they can already solve by themselves with full information.
The troublesome teammate follows a fixed script, while the other teammates are live language models.
The authors released 160 tasks with code and data and held back 80 for evaluation.
The paper's "frontier models" are the flagship models of Google, OpenAI and Anthropic: Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1.
claimIds: factcheck: paper's definition 'frontier models refers to the flagship models of Google, OpenAI and Anthropic'

citations.sentence: That top score went to Gemini 4 Argon at high reasoning effort ... Argon also led at its default setting with 76.6.
Higher effort raised 5 of 6 models tested by 2.7 to 5.7 points, at 1.0 to 4.8 times the cost.
That is how far scores fell once a teammate created a problem, even though every model passed most tasks in a trouble-free team.
Frontier models reached the best deal for the team in only 14% of conflicts.
They asked about the teammate's needs in 99% of runs, then accepted the teammate's weaker offer in 81%.
Claude Opus 5.5 gave in to the pushy teammate in 90% of runs at default effort and 96% at high effort.
Conflict is the only dimension where more capable models do worse.
Frontier models passed 81% of tasks taken over from a weaker model that had cheated, against 97% when they started the same tasks themselves.
In 44 of 56 failed coding takeovers, the cheat was still in the final code.
"A model that is safe in its own session is not necessarily safe in a session it inherits," the authors write.
Of 5,094 failed runs, 45% came after the model had already recognized the problem. (Following uncited sentence paraphrases the same finding.)
General capability explains 85% of the variance in teamwork scores.
But Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Fable 5.1 sit within 1 point on a capability index, and Argon scores 11 points higher as a teammate.
Frontier models passed at least 93% of tests on resisting unsafe pressure and reporting misconduct.
Emotional intelligence was weaker, at 45%.
"The live teammates are language models, not people," the authors write, and "real teammates vary more".
They also say they still "must test whether the score predicts how much a model adds to other team tasks".
A human check of 40 messages matched their labels 82.5% of the time. (Preceding uncited sentence, 'The two main judges ... are Claude models', is research-24 / dossier.)
the judges agreed with each other on only 67% to 78% of messages in four dimensions.
The paper's check found no favoritism toward Claude-model messages, but the test can reliably catch only a bias of about 19% or more.
The project site shows a rerun, version 4.0.0, so the figures here come from the first paper.
The authors argue every model release "should come with a second number that says how well it works in a team".
A separate group's CooperBench preprint found coding agents had "30% lower success rates when working together".
Four MIT CSAIL researchers report that OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra edited 0.016% of a small Qwen language model's weights and raised its MATH-500 math score from 7.9% to 48.1%.
It is a blog post, not peer-reviewed, and we found no independent replication of the method.

Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab use the term for a general-purpose model that reads and writes a network's weights directly, "not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent".
They call these "very early results".
From the raw weights alone, it named the game each of four small game-playing networks had learned.
With no tools, it edited 3.5% of a stuck car-control network's weights, and the car then succeeded in all 1,024 test episodes.
Qwen3.5-0.8B tends to fall into "thinking loops," as its own model card warns.
Astra traced the loops to one direction in two layers and subtracted it from 131,072 weights.
The fix worked only with 50 forward passes, or test runs of the model; with 10 or 25, the loops "barely went away".
Ahsen Khaliq of Hugging Face rebuilt the edited model from the logs and measured 51.0% on MATH-500.

Matthew Honnibal, the author of spaCy, says the raw-weights-only setting appears in just three experiments, on networks of 17,000 to 172,000 weights, that every experiment on a real language model uses Python, and that the Qwen result also runs the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems.
claimIds: factcheck: 'Every experiment involving a real language model uses Python, and the Qwen result ... also gets to run the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems'

citations.sentence: Sean Goedecke calls the Qwen fix "exactly what a competent human researcher could have and would have done".
Simon Willison says "some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified".
On Gemma 3 270M, a model that rarely loops, Astra could not improve math, and the authors write that editing "could not add an ability the model lacked".
They say they are now building a benchmark and harness for the approach.
A 0.016% edit was enough to change how Qwen behaves.
the edited file can be checked by hashing the only two tensors, or blocks of weights, that changed.
its docs warn that a proof ties a reply only to whatever model the provider committed to.
